evals.name: ring-vs-tree-tradeoff
evals.prompt: NCCL all-reduce에서 ring이랑 tree가 뭐가 달라? 언제 뭘 쓰는 거야?
evals.expected_output: Ring: bandwidth-optimal 2(n-1)S/n but latency 2(n-1)*alpha linear in n. Tree: ~2*log2(n)*alpha latency, so wins for small/medium messages at large n. NCCL picks by size and world size.

assertions.description: States ring achieves the bandwidth lower bound, moving about 2(n−1)S/n bytes per rank
States ring's latency term is 2(n−1)·α, i.e. linear in the number of ranks
States the tree/double-binary-tree latency is about 2·log₂(n)·α, logarithmic in n
Explains double binary trees as building a second tree where the first tree's leaves become internal nodes, so every rank both sends and receives
Says trees win for small/medium messages and rings for large messages where bandwidth dominates

evals.name: busbw-vs-algbw
evals.prompt: nccl-tests를 돌렸더니 algbw가 8 GB/s인데 우리 링크는 200 Gb/s짜리야. 이거 문제 있는 거야?
evals.expected_output: Converts 200 Gb/s to 25 GB/s; explains algbw vs busbw and applies the 2(n-1)/n correction for all-reduce before comparing to link speed.

assertions.description: Converts the vendor's 200 Gb/s to 25 GB/s by dividing by 8
Distinguishes algbw (S/T, what the application sees) from busbw (what the wire carries)
States the all-reduce busbw correction factor is 2(n−1)/n and applies it before comparing to link speed
Says busbw, not algbw, is the number to compare against the hardware, because algbw never reaches line rate

evals.name: timeout-means-a-rank-missing
evals.prompt: Our job died with 'Watchdog caught collective operation timeout'. Should I just increase the NCCL timeout?
evals.expected_output: No. A collective is a barrier, so a timeout means some rank never arrived. Ranks the causes by base rate starting with divergent control flow, and describes flight-recorder localization.

assertions.description: Advises against simply raising the timeout as the fix
States that a collective is a barrier, so a timeout means some rank never arrived at it, not that the network is slow
Notes the rank that reported the timeout is one that DID arrive, so the culprit is a silent rank
Names divergent control flow (a rank skipping or taking a different branch, or an unequal dataloader length) as the most common cause
Describes using the flight recorder / trace buffer and comparing collective sequence numbers across ranks to find which rank is behind

evals.name: bucket-size-derivation
evals.prompt: Why does gradient bucketing help, and how should I pick the bucket size?
evals.expected_output: k(alpha+beta*s) vs alpha+beta*k*s saves (k-1)*alpha; bucket must exceed S*=alpha/beta but stay small enough to leave overlap window; ~25MB default.

assertions.description: Uses the α + β·S cost model explicitly
Shows the saving from bucketing is about (k−1)·α, the amortized per-message latency
Notes the bucket should be larger than the latency/bandwidth crossover S* = α/β
Notes a too-large bucket delays the start of communication and shrinks the overlap window with backward compute

evals.name: checkpoint-interval-math
evals.prompt: 체크포인트 저장에 120초 걸리고, job 단위 MTBF가 3시간이야. 얼마나 자주 저장해야 최적이야?
evals.expected_output: T_opt = sqrt(2*C*MTBF) = sqrt(2*120*10800) ~ 1610s ~ 27 min, with ~15% overhead split evenly between write cost and lost work.

assertions.description: States the optimal interval as T_opt ≈ sqrt(2·C·MTBF)
Computes a numeric answer of roughly 1600 seconds / about 25–30 minutes
Notes that at the optimum the checkpoint-write cost and the expected lost work are equal
Attributes the result to Young/Daly rather than presenting it as a rule of thumb

evals.name: overlap-broken-diagnosis
evals.prompt: My profile shows all the NCCL kernels running in one long block after the backward pass finishes, instead of overlapping. I'm using gradient accumulation. What's wrong?
evals.expected_output: Missing no_sync() on the first m-1 micro-batches so an all-reduce fires every micro-batch; also lists host syncs, find_unused_parameters, and global grad clipping.

assertions.description: Identifies missing no_sync() (or equivalent) under gradient accumulation as the likely cause
Explains that without it an all-reduce fires every micro-batch, costing m times the expected communication
Lists at least one other overlap breaker such as a host sync (.item()/.cpu()), find_unused_parameters=True, or global gradient clipping before the reduce
Describes what a healthy profile looks like: NCCL kernels interleaved with backward compute, with only the last bucket exposed
